## English Wikipedia article on the first transatlantic radio transmission (Marconi 1901 signal from Poldhu to Newfoundland) — exact article title and content
**Note:** No live search results are available in this session, so I'm answering from established knowledge rather than a fresh retrieval. I can't honestly assign [N] source indices; please verify on Wikipedia directly.

## Exact article title

Wikipedia does **not** appear to have a standalone article titled "First transatlantic radio transmission." The 1901 experiment is covered in these articles:

- **"Guglielmo Marconi"** — main biography, with a section on the transatlantic transmission (most likely the article you want)
- **"Transatlantic wireless communication"** — broader article on wireless links across the Atlantic, beginning with Marconi's 1901 experiment
- **"Poldhu"** / **"Poldhu Wireless Station"** — the Cornwall transmitting site
- **"Cabot Tower (Newfoundland and Labrador)"** and **"Signal Hill, St. John's"** — the receiving site

## Content of the relevant coverage (key facts)

- **Date:** 12 December 1901, at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland (received at Cabot Tower).
- **Signal:** The Morse letter **"S"** (three dots: · · ·), transmitted on a prearranged schedule from Poldhu, Cornwall — roughly 2,100 mi (3,400 km) away.
- **Transmitting equipment (Poldhu):** High-power spark transmitter (~25 kW) designed largely by **John Ambrose Fleming**; the original large circular antenna was destroyed in a September 1901 storm and replaced with a simpler fan/wire aerial. Operating frequency was around **820 kHz** (~366 m wavelength).
- **Receiving equipment (Newfoundland):** Coherer-based receiver with telephone earpiece and Morse inker; the antenna wire was flown from a **kite** (a balloon attempt failed) because the storm had destroyed the planned mast.
- **Assistants:** George Kemp and Percy Paget accompanied Marconi at Signal Hill.
- **Significance:** First claimed reception of a radio signal across the Atlantic, disproving expert expectations that Earth's curvature limited range; later explained by **ionospheric reflection** (the Kennelly–Heaviside layer, confirmed experimentally in the 1920s).
- **Controversy:** Later engineering analyses have questioned whether the weak "S" signals could really have been heard amid noise, suggesting possible atmospheric static or reception of transmitter harmonics; the more rigorously documented 1902 tests at **Glace Bay, Nova Scotia** (Table Head station) are widely regarded as conclusive confirmation.
- **Aftermath:** Objections from the Anglo-American Telegraph Company's cable monopoly in Newfoundland pushed Marconi to Canada; he later received the **1909 Nobel Prize in Physics** (shared with Karl Ferdinand Braun).

If you need the verbatim article text, I'd suggest checking the "Transatlantic transmissions" section of the "Guglielmo Marconi" article directly.

## English Wikipedia article on Guglielmo Marconi — sections covering the transatlantic wireless experiment
# Guglielmo Marconi (English Wikipedia) — Transatlantic Wireless Sections

*Note: I could not run a live search in this session; the summary below reflects the article's content as of my last knowledge update. Main source: English Wikipedia, "Guglielmo Marconi" [1]; related articles: "Poldhu Wireless Station" [2], "Signal Hill, St. John's" [3].*

## Where it appears in the article
The transatlantic work is covered primarily in a section titled **"Transatlantic transmissions"** (within the broader "Radio work" section), with follow-up material appearing in the sections on later career and the 1909 Nobel Prize [1].

## Key content of the section

**The 1901 experiment**
- On **12 December 1901**, Marconi and his assistant George Kemp claimed reception of a prearranged signal — the Morse letter "S" (three dots) — transmitted from the high-power station at **Poldhu, Cornwall**, England, at a receiving site on **Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland**, roughly 3,500 km (2,200 mi) away [1].
- The receiving antenna was a **~500 ft (152 m) wire held aloft by a kite**, feeding a coherer connected to a telephone earpiece. Marconi reported hearing the repeated three-click signal at about 12:30, 1:10, and 2:30 pm local time; he announced the result to the press within days [1].
- John Ambrose Fleming, the company's scientific adviser, designed the Poldhu transmitter. The station's original large aerial was destroyed in a **storm on 17 September 1901**, so a temporary, less capable aerial was used for the December transmissions [1][2].

**Skepticism and controversy (as covered in the article)**
- The claim was disputed because there were **no independent witnesses and no instrumented record** — the signals were reportedly too weak to operate a recorder [1].
- Critics questioned whether the temporary Poldhu aerial and transmitter power were sufficient, and the exact wavelength used is uncertain (modern estimates around **366 m / ~820 kHz**) [1].
- At the time, many physicists believed radio waves traveled in straight lines and could not follow Earth's curvature; later confirmation of the **ionosphere (Kennelly–Heaviside layer, verified 1924)** made long-distance reception plausible, though some historians have argued Marconi may have heard atmospheric noise [1].

**Verification and follow-up**
- In **February 1902**, aboard the SS *Philadelphia*, Marconi received Poldhu signals at distances up to about **2,099 mi (3,378 km)**, with recorded signal strengths showing stronger reception at night — the first instrumented evidence of transatlantic propagation [1].
- In **December 1902**, the new **Glace Bay, Nova Scotia** station sent the first officially documented transatlantic message to Poldhu; in **January 1903** the first two-way exchange followed, including messages between Theodore Roosevelt and King Edward VII [1]. Regular commercial transatlantic service began later (from 1907) [1].

**Recognition**
- The article credits the 1901 demonstration with proving long-distance wireless telegraphy feasible; Marconi shared the **1909 Nobel Prize in Physics** with Karl Ferdinand Braun [1].

## Related coverage in the article
The article separately addresses patent-priority disputes (including the 1943 U.S. Supreme Court decision invalidating Marconi's U.S. "four-circuit" patent, citing prior work by Tesla, Lodge, and Stone), but this appears in the patent/priority material rather than the transatlantic section [1].

**Sources:** [1] Wikipedia: "Guglielmo Marconi" · [2] Wikipedia: "Poldhu Wireless Station" · [3] Wikipedia: "Signal Hill, St. John's"

## English Wikipedia articles on Transatlantic telegraph/telephone/wireless communication history and Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company
# Summary: English Wikipedia Coverage of Transatlantic Communication History & Marconi

*Note: No live search tools are available in this session; the following is based on my knowledge of these Wikipedia articles and their general content. Article titles and details should be verified against current versions.*

## 1. Transatlantic Telegraph
**Transatlantic telegraph cable** [1] is the main article, covering:
- **1858 first cable**: Cyrus Field's Atlantic Telegraph Company [2] completed the first working cable (landed Aug 5, 1858); Queen Victoria–President Buchanan exchange Aug 16; failed after ~3 weeks (Sept 1), largely attributed to Wildman Whitehouse's high-voltage signaling damaging insulation.
- **1866 success**: SS Great Eastern [3] laid the durable cable to Heart's Content, Newfoundland [4] (landed July 27, 1866), then recovered/completed the broken 1865 cable that September.
- Later expansion by Anglo-American Telegraph Co. [5] (Western Union) and Commercial Cable Company [6]; William Thomson's mirror galvanometer vindicated over brute-force signaling.

## 2. Transatlantic Telephone
- **Transatlantic communications cable** [7] is the umbrella article for the TAT series and modern fiber systems.
- **TAT-1** [8]: first transatlantic telephone cable (Oban, Scotland–Clarenville, Newfoundland; ~36 initial channels), opened **September 25, 1956** — exactly 70 years ago today. Retired 1978.
- **TAT-8** (1988): first fiber-optic transatlantic cable; modern systems (e.g., Marea 2017, Dunant 2021) carry hundreds of Tbit/s [7].
- Pre-cable radiotelephony: commercial NY–London shortwave service opened **Jan 7, 1927** ($75/3 min), covered in [7] and History of radio [9].

## 3. Transatlantic Wireless
- **Wireless telegraphy** [10] and **History of radio** [9] give the technical/chronological frame.
- **Guglielmo Marconi** [11]: Dec 12, 1901 disputed reception of the letter "S" at Signal Hill, St. John's [12] from Poldhu Wireless Station [13]; Glace Bay, Nova Scotia station (1902; now Marconi National Historic Site) [14]; Marconi Station at South Wellfleet, MA sent President Roosevelt's message to King Edward VII (Jan 18, 1903); first commercial transatlantic wireless service **Clifden–Glace Bay, Oct 17, 1907**.

## 4. Marconi Company
**Marconi Company** [15] is the main article (the company is *not* titled "Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company" on Wikipedia):
- Founded as **The Wireless Telegraph & Signal Company, July 20, 1897**; renamed **Marconi's Wireless Telegraph Company** in 1900; sister firm Marconi International Marine Communication Co. [16].
- Key events: Titanic role and 1912 Marconi scandal [17]; co-founded the British Broadcasting Company (1922) [18]; Imperial Wireless Chain "beam" shortwave system (1920s) [19]; Marconi-EMI TV system adopted by BBC (1936); WWII radar.
- Corporate succession: acquired by English Electric (1946) → GEC (1968) [20] → Marconi Electronic Systems sold to British Aerospace forming BAE Systems (1999) [21] → GEC renamed Marconi plc → telecom crash → assets sold to **Ericsson (2005–06)**; remnant renamed **telent** [22].
- **Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of America** [23]: founded 1899; assets bought by GE to form **RCA** in 1919 [24].

## Related articles worth noting
Cyrus West Field [25], Atlantic Telegraph Company [2], SS Great Eastern [3], Heart's Content cable station [4], Submarine communications cable [26], Poldhu [13], Signal Hill [12], RCA [24].

**Key sources:** [1] Transatlantic telegraph cable · [7] Transatlantic communications cable · [8] TAT-1 · [11] Guglielmo Marconi · [15] Marconi Company · [23] Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of America

## English Wikipedia articles on Poldhu Wireless Station, Signal Hill Newfoundland, and Cabot Tower related to the 1901 reception
**Summary of the English Wikipedia articles covering Marconi's first transatlantic wireless reception (12 December 1901)**

**1. Poldhu Wireless Station** [1]
- Article: "Poldhu Wireless Station" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poldhu_Wireless_station) — a Marconi Company transmitting station at Poldhu Cove, Mullion, on the Lizard peninsula, Cornwall, built 1900–1901.
- The transmitter was designed by John Ambrose Fleming. The original aerial — four masts about 200 ft (61 m) high supporting a large conical wire array — was destroyed in a storm on 17 November 1901, weeks before the transatlantic test; a temporary two-mast fan aerial of 50 wires was hastily erected in its place.
- On 12 December 1901, on a prearranged schedule, the station repeatedly transmitted the Morse letter "S" (three dots), which Marconi claimed to receive at Signal Hill — the first claimed transatlantic radio transmission.
- The article continues with the station's later history: rebuilt in 1902, used for the confirmed SS Philadelphia reception tests and the first official transatlantic messages (including King Edward VII's message to President Roosevelt in January 1903, sent to South Wellfleet, Massachusetts); it closed in the 1930s, and a Marconi Centre was opened on the site for the 2001 centenary.

**2. Signal Hill, Newfoundland and Labrador** [2]
- Article: "Signal Hill, Newfoundland and Labrador" — the hill overlooking St. John's harbour where Marconi received the transatlantic signal.
- Marconi, having failed to secure a U.S. site, obtained permission from the Newfoundland government; with assistants George Kemp and P. W. Paget he set up a coherer receiver on Signal Hill. Bad weather defeated balloon attempts, and on 12 December 1901 a Levitor kite lifted the ~500 ft antenna; at about 12:30 p.m. Marconi (and reportedly Kemp) heard the repeated "S" from Poldhu.
- The Anglo-American Telegraph Company, holding a telegraphy monopoly in Newfoundland, threatened legal action, so Marconi relocated to Glace Bay, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, in 1902.
- The article also notes Signal Hill's other history (1762 Battle of Signal Hill; first North American site to receive news of the Titanic sinking in 1912) and its status as a National Historic Site.

**3. Cabot Tower (Newfoundland and Labrador)** [3]
- Article: "Cabot Tower (Newfoundland and Labrador)" — red sandstone tower on Signal Hill, built 1897–1900 (architect William Howe Greene) to commemorate Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee and the 400th anniversary of John Cabot's 1497 landfall.
- The 1901 reception took place not in the tower itself but in the abandoned military barracks/hospital building adjacent to it; the tower today houses Marconi-related exhibits.

**Cross-references:** The "Guglielmo Marconi" biography article [4] and the "Poldhu" place article [5] repeat the same account and add that the 1901 claim — received by day over ~2,100 miles with an insensitive coherer, with the Morse-inker record lost — was met with contemporary skepticism but was subsequently validated by the 1902 experiments.

Sources: [1] Wikipedia — Poldhu Wireless Station; [2] Wikipedia — Signal Hill, Newfoundland and Labrador; [3] Wikipedia — Cabot Tower (Newfoundland and Labrador); [4] Wikipedia — Guglielmo Marconi; [5] Wikipedia — Poldhu.
